cia-0000119212:
An April 1984 CIA document lays out what the American intelligence community was doing about the prisoner and missing problem. By the mid-1980s the search for answers had become a standing mission with its own staff and routines. Several agencies shared the work, and this paper describes their actions.

Inside, the document divides duties and reports steps taken across the community. That kind of coordination paper shows how a wartime question became a long bureaucratic effort. It matters because it explains the machinery behind the searches, the briefings, and the reports to families that continued for years after the last troops came home.
cia-0000132412: Cuban developments are surveyed in a CIA document dated September 5, 1959. Eight months had passed since Castro's victory, and the revolution was still defining itself week by week. Washington watched every turn of the new regime with close attention. The short document gathers the latest changes as the agency saw them that autumn, while Cuba's final direction was still being argued over in Havana.
cia-0000132512:
Parochial schools being seized by the Castro regime fill a CIA item dated April 4, 1961. The headline also reports foreign priests being expelled, though the last word is cut short in the record. The revolution was moving directly against the Catholic Church that spring.

The item reports the seizures and expulsions as they were announced. Church schools had educated much of Cuba's middle class for generations. For readers, the entry marks a sharp break between the regime and one of the island's oldest bodies. It came days before the Bay of Pigs invasion hardened every line in Cuba.
cia-0000132612: A Lima meeting of left-of-center parties calling for unity fills item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the word united, leaving the call unfinished. Peru's capital was hosting the region's moderate left that month. The short item reports the meeting and what the parties agreed to demand.
cia-0000135812: Weekly progress reports fill a CIA paper from 1954 on the Guatemala operation. Part of its headline subject was deleted before release. The reports cover the week of March 23 through 29, though the headline breaks off mid-word. A weekly rhythm ran through the whole covert campaign that year. The short paper keeps the reports for that week as filed.
cia-0000135912: Dated 5 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records a short summary of a meeting held on 17 June, cabled from Guatemala City under a May date. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136112: With a date of 3 April 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a visit by Salamander to Sherwood. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136312: Sent to SKILLET, ONTRICH, and SHERWOOD in June 1954, this LINCOLN cable passes on the latest reliable situation report from PBSUCCESS. Liberation forces had captured Chiquimula the day before, were joyfully received, and were advancing toward Zacapa, while aircraft damaged trains carrying troop reinforcements. Guatemala City's petroleum stocks were dwindling after bomb damage, with only days of supply left. The cable also flags talking points for each recipient's audience.
cia-0000136912: Learn all you can about an arms shipment, this April 1954 cable directs. A Swedish ship delivered the arms at Puerto Barrios, Guatemala. A contact in Stockholm is to be asked for aid. The cargo is to be checked in full. The man on the spot may travel to make contact. Much of the text is garbled. But the target is clear. It is the shipment that became the Alfhem affair. That Czech arms delivery sharpened the crisis before the invasion.
un-ga-res-12: Staff who had run the UN's stopgap office in its first weeks needed word on their future. Resolution 12, passed on 1 February 1946, praises their able and faithful service. It lets the Secretary-General keep them on, under present terms, until 1 April 1946, or until he can sign them to new terms under the draft staff rules. The move also guards his free hand to pick the lasting staff.
un-ga-res-112:
Korea's future came before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 112, adopted on 14 November 1947. Korea had been freed from Japanese rule in 1945, then split between Soviet and U.S. forces. The Assembly holds that the Korean question belongs first of all to the Korean people, and that it touches their freedom and self-rule. No fair answer can be found, it says, without Koreans in the room.

Elected Korean voices are to be invited to take part in the debate. The Assembly sets up a UN Temporary Commission on Korea. Its job: make sure those voices are truly picked by the people, not named by the army chiefs on the ground. The commission may travel, watch, and consult across the whole land.
un-ga-res-712:
Guns fell silent in Korea in the summer of 1953, and the UN General Assembly marked the moment in Resolution 712, approved on 28 August 1953. The text recalls the chain of Security Council and Assembly votes that began with the North Korean attack of June 1950. It takes note of the report of the Unified Command, dated 7 August 1953, sent after the truce was signed.

The Assembly salutes the brave troops of the Republic of Korea and of all states that sent forces to aid it. It honors those who died fighting back the attack, in defense of freedom and peace. The vote calls the war the first proof that joint defense under the Charter can work.
un-ga-res-2012:
Threats of a breakaway in Southern Rhodesia drew Resolution 2012, adopted by the General Assembly on 12 October 1965. The white regime in the British colony kept vowing to declare itself free at once, in order to keep minority rule in place for good. Britain, the ruling power, held that such a move would be rebellion, and any act to give it force would be treason.

The Assembly condemns any bid by the Rhodesian chiefs to seize freedom by unlawful means. Lasting minority rule, it says, clashes with the Charter's pledge of equal rights and with the 1960 call to end colonial rule. The vote came one month before the regime did declare itself free, on 11 November 1965.
un-ga-res-a-69-12: Joint work with a security bloc of former Soviet states fills Resolution A/69/12, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Collective Security Treaty Organization has held observer status at the Assembly since 2004. Past votes of 2010 and 2012 framed the tie. A joint pledge of the two bodies' staffs, signed in April 2010, is recalled, as is the Assembly's 1994 call for stronger UN work with regional groups.
un-sc-res-12: Four Balkan states were called to speak, without a vote, under Security Council Resolution 12 of 1946. Greece and Yugoslavia are invited to take part in the Council's talks in full. Albania and Bulgaria are invited so the Council can hear such words as they wish to give. If the matter later proves to be a true dispute, the last two will gain the same right to sit in on the talks. The vote is a small step in the Greek border fight that then filled the Council's plate.
un-sc-res-312: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 312, catalogued under 1972. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-412: Filed in the official record under number 412, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 2021 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1312: The catalog's entries for 2000 include Resolution 1312 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1712: Resolution 1712, from 2006, is a formal act of the Security Council preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its opening clauses do the framing work, naming the situation and the principles at stake. Its closing clauses do the deciding. The entry holds the whole arc, which is what gives a resolution its force.
un-sc-res-1812: Adopted in 2008, Resolution 1812 is part of the Security Council's numbered record kept in this collection through English Wikisource. The act follows the standard internal order: matters recalled, facts noted with concern or welcome, steps decided. The preservation of the whole order matters, because the decisions only make sense standing on their stated grounds.

plos-pone-0000012:
Don Klinkenberg, Christophe Fraser, and Hans Heesterbeek asked in 2006 how well contact tracing really works when a new epidemic breaks out. Contact tracing means finding the people an infected person has exposed, then isolating or treating them before they spread the disease further. It is slow, costly work.

Using models of emerging infections, the team tested when tracing can hold an outbreak down and when it falls behind. Speed, the share of contacts found, and how fast the disease spreads all change the answer. Their results help health officials judge whether tracing is worth its heavy cost in the first weeks of an epidemic, the moment when control is still possible.
cia-0000137312: Dated 1961, NSC Briefing — Cuba is a declassified CIA paper written for the National Security Council on the state of affairs in Cuba. The year matters: 1961 brought the Bay of Pigs landing in April and a hard freeze in U.S.–Cuban relations. The catalog does not date the briefing more closely or name its topics, so this description does not place it before or after the landing. It stands as one of the Cuba briefings prepared for the council in that crisis year, released through the CIA Reading Room.
un-sc-res-212:
Security Council Resolution 212, adopted on September 20, 1965, recommended the Maldives for membership in the United Nations. The island chain in the Indian Ocean had gained full independence from Britain less than two months before, on July 26. Its government moved fast to take a place in the world body alongside other new states of the decade.

The Assembly seated the Maldives the next day, making it one of the smallest members of the time. The resolution follows the usual pattern: a finding that the applicant accepts the Charter, then a referral to the Assembly. For a nation of scattered atolls, membership gave a voice far beyond its size.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d12: On June 25, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt again, five days after his previous message in this series. The new note is Document 12 of the Cairo and Tehran volume in the Foreign Relations record. Late June brought allied argument over where to strike next in the Mediterranean, but the record for this item names no subject. The text itself, printed in full in the volume, is the only sound source for its errand.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d112: On November 10, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill, two days before sailing aboard the battleship Iowa. The letter is Document 112 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Final letters before a wartime voyage tended to mix the practical with the strategic, though this record names no topic. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, at the point where the correspondence gives way to the journey itself.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d212:
A State Department memorandum dated at Moscow on 11 November 1943 sets out how Germany should be treated once it surrenders. Drawn up for the three big Allies to agree in advance, it starts from the declared aim of Germany's unconditional surrender.

The draft surrender terms demand an admission of total defeat, signed by both the German government and its military chiefs, with the Allies holding all the rights of an occupying power. Political prisoners must be freed, the camps emptied, and accused war criminals handed over. During the armistice, an inter-Allied Control Commission would rule Germany, British, Soviet, and American troops would occupy it, and Nazi officials at every level would be removed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d312:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued a secret note, paper C.C.S. 409, at Cairo on 25 November 1943 under the heading Overlord and the Mediterranean. It names the central quarrel of the Sextant Conference: how far the sanctity of Overlord must be preserved whole, whatever happens in the Mediterranean.

Much has changed since Quebec, the British argue: Russia advances beyond hope, Italy is out of the war, and Turkey may soon join. They do not recoil from a cross-Channel attack in late spring or early summer of 1944, but they refuse to treat a fixed date as the pivot of all strategy. German strength in France might make Overlord impossible, or make an early Rankin landing essential. Their policy is to stretch German forces everywhere and strike wherever the Allies hold superiority, letting Overlord follow from that pressure.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d412:
Howard Bucknell, counselor of the American embassy in London, sent the Secretary of State a short telegram, number 8476, on 4 December 1943. It reports how the news of the Tehran Conference reached the British public that morning.

Moscow radio's announcement of the conference, Bucknell writes, is carried in the late editions of the morning's London papers, though it arrived too late for editorial comment. Speculative stories over the past two days, he notes, had rested largely on a German press and radio campaign meant to prepare enemy populations for the expected news of the meeting. Senator Connally's speech at Fort Worth, in which he had spoken openly of a great conference in the Middle East, was also widely reported in Britain.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d512:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on December 9, 1943, three days after the Second Cairo Conference closed. The two leaders had spent most of a month traveling and conferring, from Cairo to Tehran and back to Cairo. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

By December 9 the alliance had settled its course for 1944, and the correspondence between the heads of government turned to carrying it out. Churchill's letters to Roosevelt mixed business, argument, and friendship in a way no later summary can reproduce. This one belongs to the immediate settling-up after the summits, when the decisions were fresh and the work was beginning.
frus-1944-quebec-d12:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 28, 1944, as Cherbourg fell to American troops in Normandy. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, in the run of pre-conference correspondence.

Late June brought the alliance a working port in France and a grinding battle for the Norman countryside. Churchill's correspondence that week balanced celebration with argument about the next moves in Italy and southern France. For readers, the message belongs to the summer when victory in the West became a matter of time, and the leaders' letters began to carry more postwar business than battle plans.
frus-1944-quebec-d112:
President Roosevelt wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on September 9, 1944, about lend-lease policy after Germany's collapse. Departments in Washington had been discussing the question on their own, and Roosevelt wanted it stopped. Identical letters went to the service chiefs, the Treasury, and the agencies that ran foreign aid and shipping.

Roosevelt ordered that no department act alone on lend-lease, since any step would affect national policy as a whole. Instructions already issued about aid after Germany fell were to be cancelled at once. He promised his own directions soon. The letter shows the president pulling a sensitive allied question back into his own hands before Quebec.
frus-1944-quebec-d212:
The only source for this conversation, the editors note, is Eden's memoir. After the press conference of September 16, 1944, the Foreign Secretary said goodbye to Roosevelt alone. The president told him that he would visit England at the end of November whether he won or lost the election. It is a small, human entry amid the conference's military paperwork.

The note's footnote confirms the plan from another source. Churchill told Stalin on September 27 that Roosevelt intended to visit England, and thereafter France and the Low Countries, immediately after the election, win or lose. The editors cite both Churchill's memoir and the published Stalin correspondence for the message.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d12: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 22 October 1944, fresh from his own trip to Moscow that month. The message survives as document 12 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Churchill often reported his impressions of Stalin to the president, and this letter belongs to that candid channel between the two Western leaders.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d112:
On 19 January 1945 the Secretary of State pressed the President for a quick decision. The paper at issue is the draft pact on control machinery for Germany. It came out of the European Advisory Commission in London. Stettinius's note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Britain gave its approval on 5 December 1944, and Soviet approval is expected at any moment. Without a word from Washington, the United States would sit in an awkward place in the commission. Stettinius notes that the heads of the War and Navy Departments both urged approval in a letter of 27 December. He asks the President to decide at the earliest chance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d212:
Washington sent Paris a warm holding answer on de Gaulle's arms letter on 27 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's cable to Ambassador Caffery, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, carries a letter to be handed to the French foreign minister. It buys time without cooling the French.

De Gaulle's letter on the further arming of French forces, the reply says, is deeply appreciated. It now lies before the United States Chiefs of Staff for their study and advice, and a firm answer may soon be possible. In the meantime, Washington fully grasps France's fervent desire to strike at Germany with all she has. French troops fighting beside their allies are making an outstanding contribution, and earlier American arming, in North Africa and since, is recalled with pride.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d312:
For one Malta meeting, no official record survives at all, and the editors of this volume say so plainly. Their short note explains where the only account can be found. It sits in Secretary Stettinius's memoir, on two pages the note cites. The session ran late, ending close to midnight.

Notes like this one mark the honest gaps in the conference record. Where the files gave out, the editors leaned on a man who was in the room and later wrote about it. Readers are told exactly how much weight the evidence can bear, and no more.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d412:
Side by side with the delegation's other draft, this invitation text of February 9, 1945, shows the wording still in motion. The draft proposes that the conference take the Dumbarton Oaks plan as the basis for a charter. A copy of that plan, it notes, had already been sent to the invited government. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d512:
The veto question follows Stettinius to San Francisco in this cable to Grew of June 3, 1945. He asks Grew to pass his message to the President. The precise issue at present, he writes, has caused great confusion, especially in the press. It is whether a great power not involved in a dispute can use the veto to block mere discussion of a situation in the Council.

Discussion, in such cases, would only let the Council decide what action, if any, to take or recommend. All agreed, Stettinius notes, that unanimity of the great powers not involved should govern substantive decisions. The cable shows Yalta's voting bargain being defended at the conference it created.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d12:
How to make Stalin ask for the meeting fills Grew's memorandum of a second conference on May 15, 1945. Eden, Balfour, Harriman, William Phillips, and Grew took part. Reference was made to a recent message from the President suggesting Stalin might take the initiative in calling the conference. Eden asked whether Truman had any idea how Stalin might be induced to do so.

Harriman thought it could readily be managed by Clark Kerr, the British ambassador. If Clark Kerr reached Moscow first, he could turn conversation so as to reveal whether Stalin would in fact take the initiative. Discussion then turned to the best place for the meeting. The extract shows diplomacy arranging even the invitation's authorship.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d112:
Robert Murphy reported the Berlin timetable agreed with Marshal Zhukov in an urgent telegram from Hoechst on June 30, 1945. The message is document 112 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Generals Clay and Weeks had met Zhukov in Berlin the day before to plan the Allied move into the occupation zones.

The Soviets want a fast Western pullback starting July 1, with the withdrawal finished by July 4 and Allied troops entering Berlin on the last day. Murphy lists the agreed steps: scouting parties first, then main bodies moving in on July 3 and 4. Free use of the Hanau-Magdeburg-Berlin highway is granted, rail lines are assigned, and traffic on approved routes will pass without border searches. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d212:
Ambassador Harriman confirmed the reparations discussion to Molotov in a letter dated July 12, 1945. The letter is document 212 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Molotov had asked about reparations when Harriman delivered the President's topic list on July 7.

Harriman explains that the President asked Pauley to come to Berlin to report on the state of the reparations commission's work in Moscow. He is satisfied, he adds, that the President will wish to discuss at the conference those reparations matters that remain unsettled. Pauley has confirmed this himself and has so informed Maisky, the Soviet chairman of the commission. The short letter locked reparations into the Potsdam program without adding it to the formal topic list.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d312:
Winant forwarded the British Foreign Office's formal reply from London on July 13, 1945. London had weighed Washington's letters of June 25 and July 9 on peace treaties with Bulgaria, Hungary, and Rumania. The reply, sent to the Department, was also repeated to Moscow.

Britain said it fully shared the wish for a real American and British part in the Control Commissions. It also wanted better political conditions in the three countries. But London confessed it still doubted the course Washington favored. The exchange shows the two allies entering Potsdam agreed on the problem, yet split on the remedy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d412:
Deadlock in London is the burden of Winant's cable of July 12, 1945. The European Advisory Commission held a long, inconclusive discussion of the new Soviet proposal on France's Berlin area. The Soviet delegation, Winant reports, had authority to conclude the French zone agreement only if its new formula was added.

The American and British representatives kept opposing any wording that stated the French area would be formed from the American and British areas alone. The French representative, Massigli, was eager to conclude the agreement on any basis the other three accepted. Winant also asks for fresh facts on destruction in Berlin, to offset Soviet claims relayed from Marshal Zhukov.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d512:
Territory Germany annexed from Poland in 1939 should simply go back, a briefing book paper of July 3, 1945 recommends. The territory of pre-war Poland annexed by Germany in 1939, it states, should be returned to Poland. Its basic data recall how Poland won that land after the first World War, through the Treaty of Versailles.

Poland then acquired the so-called Corridor, the Poznań area, and the major part of the Upper Silesian industrial area. President Wilson had played a prominent role in establishing an independent Poland with its outlet to the sea. Yet the United States, in its separate treaty with Germany of 1921, disclaimed any obligation for the territorial provisions of Versailles. The land had been a source of friction from 1919 to 1939.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d612:
An extract from Ambassador Harriman's Moscow wire of July 12, 1945, forms document 612 in the Potsdam papers. Addressed to the President and the Secretary of State, it is cut from the fuller report printed as document 577. It keeps one exchange from China's talks with Stalin.

In the passage kept here, T. V. Soong suggests going back to Chungking. He wants to consult the Generalissimo on the points still open in the Moscow talks. Stalin answers that a deal is better reached before he meets Truman at Berlin. He wishes to settle with Truman the date of Soviet entry into the war against Japan. The short extract thus ties the stalled China talks straight to the Potsdam timetable. What Soong could not close in Moscow, Stalin meant to settle with the President himself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-12:
Thompson's minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 18, 1945, at 11 a.m. at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Byrnes took the chair at Molotov's proposal, and the Council of Foreign Ministers was the business.

Molotov raised China again, but softened his objection with a condition. If the council dealt with more than European affairs alone, his doubts on China would drop. Byrnes proposed a five-power council with China's part limited in a set way. China would sit for Far Eastern problems and for questions of worldwide significance. That design, he argued, would leave a body ready for the peace in the Far East when the Japan war ended. Eden replied that for European work alone he would prefer four members.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-112:
Delegation staff drafted this working paper at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It belongs to the layer of rough texts beneath the conference's formal acts. Working papers let specialists shape options before ministers saw them. This one remained in the American files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

The interest of a working paper is its openness. Choices not yet narrowed stay visible on the page. Readers can compare its lines with the texts the conference finally approved. That comparison shows how bargaining trims a draft. The paper is a small window into the craft of writing agreements.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d712:
Document 712 is the report of the Subcommittee on the Council of Foreign Ministers, dated July 18, 1945. The council was a new body the Big Three meant to create. It would draft peace treaties and carry work between summits. A subcommittee settled its shape early in the conference. The report entered the second Potsdam volume.

Few Potsdam ideas lasted as long as this council. It met for years and framed the postwar talks. Readers find here its birth certificate: who would sit, and what work it would take. The report shows the conference building tools for the future, not just dividing the spoils of the past.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d812:
Schuyler wrote to the War Department from Rumania on July 24, 1945, in document 812. The chief of the American military team on the Rumanian control commission reported mid-conference. His channel ran to the Army, not the State Department. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Military reports from the commissions have a harder edge. Schuyler wrote of orders, movements, and obstructions in plain terms. Readers see joint occupation as soldiers lived it. The document pairs with the diplomats' Rumanian letters to give a fuller picture. Together they show a country being pulled east, reported by men watching it happen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d912: Edwin Pauley sent this urgent telegram from Babelsberg on July 22, 1945, to his reparations delegation in Moscow. He asks for four more sets of figures at once. The team must estimate the value of industrial and mining output in the Russian zone in 1938. They must also estimate farm production in that zone for the same year. Pauley wants each figure as a share of total prewar German production. He also asks what share of German industrial and mining output came from east of the Oder-Neisse rivers in 1939.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1012: Walter Brown, special assistant to the Secretary of State, passed on a late-night Soviet message in this note of July 29, 1945. At 11:35 that night, Pavlov had called with word from Stalin. The Soviet leader named his two men for the committee on disposal of the German fleet. They are Admiral of the Fleet Kuznetsov and Mr. Sobolev. Brown's memorandum is only a few lines long. It simply asks that the appointments be transmitted to Secretary Byrnes, and the file copy is an unsigned carbon.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1112:
Washington answered its Rome embassy in this message of 19 July 1945, sent by the Acting Secretary of State to Ambassador Kirk in Italy. It followed two days after Kirk's own dispatch to Washington. The channel between the capital and the Rome post ran both ways through the summit.

Messages of this kind carried orders, answers, or fresh guidance as Italy policy was adjusted in real time. The quick turn shows choices being shaped while Potsdam was still in session. Read beside Kirk's reports, this message is the home office half of a running exchange. Together they show how one country's file was handled day by day.

pmc-13447712: Blood pressure that swings wildly over 24 hours may be riskier than a steady high reading, but measuring that variability reliably is its own challenge. Stories tell of Vishnu's earthly incarnations, including Rama and Krishna, woven together with cosmology, royal genealogies, and moral teaching. Readers move from creation of the universe down through ages of kings and heroes. For students of Hindu tradition, the Purana shows how myth, history, and instruction were held together in one vast sacred account.

J. Manning Potts gathered prayers from across the Middle Ages in Prayers of the Middle Ages, letting medieval faith speak in its own voice. Monks' devotions and saints' litanies stand beside the intimate bedside prayers of ordinary believers. The arrangement suits daily use across the church year.

Short prayers for morning, danger, sickness, and death show what medieval Christians actually asked for, feared, and loved. Latin devotion survives here in English dress, often simple enough for private reading. For modern readers, the collection works two ways: as a treasury for anyone who prays, and as direct evidence of everyday religion a thousand years ago.

David Hume published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739, attempting a science of human nature built from the ground up. The mind, he argues, is a bundle of perceptions, with no simple, separate self underneath. Causation itself becomes mere habit: we expect the sun to rise because it always has, not because reason proves it must.

Reason appears as passion's slave, able to serve ends it cannot choose. Hume complained the book fell dead-born from the press, yet Kant later credited it with waking him from dogmatic slumber. Readers meet empiricism's boldest statement, written by a young Scot whose calm conclusions remain radical.

Griffith keeps one music throughout: brisk, bright, and singable, even when the Sanskrit is dark. Notes stay light so the poetry leads.
