Walter Evans-Wentz, an American scholar of religion, edited and published The Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927. Its Tibetan source, the Bardo Thodol, is a guide read aloud to the dying and the dead. Evans-Wentz worked with Tibetan teachers to render it in English.

The text leads the soul through the bardo, the state between death and rebirth, past peaceful and wrathful visions. It teaches that these visions are projections of the mind, to be recognized rather than feared. The book gave Western readers their first wide look at Tibetan Buddhism and shaped how the West thinks about death.
tob-0039-d12:
The seventeenth roll of the Doctors' Trial microfilm carries the Nuremberg transcript further through the 1946 to 1947 proceedings. Nazi physicians and health officials stood accused of crimes in the name of medicine. Their trial was recorded word for word and filmed for the archive.

Sessions preserved here add more testimony, affidavits, and documentary proof to the tribunal's growing file. The record's bulk is the story: a court drowning a crime in evidence until judgment could rest on fact. Researchers use rolls like this one to trace single witnesses, exhibits, and arguments across the whole case, which closed with the Nuremberg Code as part of its legacy.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-12:
The second part of Tract Baba Metzia fills volume twelve of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud. Part one covered finds, deposits, and wages; the debate now presses deeper into trade. The tractate's name means the Middle Gate, between the damage law before it and the property law after.

Usury rules take the front: what counts as forbidden interest, and how honest profit differs from it. Then come sales, leases of fields and houses, and the duties of neighbors sharing a courtyard wall. The rabbis argue from real contracts and real quarrels. The volume rounds out the Talmud's fullest picture of daily commerce.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-12:
Chrysostom's homilies on Paul's two letters to the Corinthians fill volume twelve of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. The Corinthian letters gave a preacher rich ground: a gifted, quarrelsome church much like Chrysostom's own. Philip Schaff edited the series.

Through forty-four homilies on the first letter and thirty on the second, he treats factions, lawsuits, marriage, and the collection for the poor. The great chapter on love gets his full rhetorical power. In the second series he defends his ministry and consoles a church under strain. Readers meet Paul filtered through the finest pulpit of the ancient world.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-12:
Leo the Great and Gregory the Great, two popes who remade their office, fill volume twelve of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Leo ruled Rome as the empire cracked in the 440s and 450s. Gregory, a century and a half later, ruled it as a plague- and war-worn city. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Leo's Tome on the two natures of Christ settled the council of Chalcedon, and his sermons and letters run the volume's first half. Gregory's pastoral rule for bishops and his letters, which managed estates, missions, and kings, fill the second. Between them, the volume shows the papacy becoming the West's steady center.
northamptonshire-witches-1612:
The Witches of Northamptonshire records a group trial held in 1612, the same summer as the famous Pendle case. Agnes Browne stands among the accused in this Jacobean pamphlet. The charges grew out of deaths and harms laid at the doors of the accused.

The pamphlet sets down the proof the court heard and the ends the accused met. Such prints let readers far away follow a trial they could never attend. They also spread stock ideas of what a witch did and how she was caught. This case ranks with the major witch trials of King James's reign.
gaufridy-life-death-aix-1612:
Louis Gaufridy served as a priest at Aix-en-Provence until the law burned him for witchcraft in 1611. The Life and Death of Lewis Gaufredy, printed in English in 1612, spread his scandal abroad. A priest accused of bewitching nuns made news far past his own town.

The account tells how young nuns at a convent were said to be seized by devils who named Gaufridy. It follows his arrest, his confession, and his death by fire. French courts treated the case as proof that no rank stood above the charge. English readers got the whole lurid tale within a year.
varro-de-re-rustica-storr-best-1912:
Marcus Terentius Varro, the most learned Roman of his age, wrote On Farming in his eightieth year. Varro on Farming, in Lloyd Storr-Best's 1912 English rendering, gives his De Re Rustica whole. The work is the oldest complete Roman book on the farm to survive.

Varro sets his lessons as talks among landowners at a country house. Crops, soils, cattle, sheep, bees, and farm hands each get their due in turn. His voice is dry, shrewd, and full of the lore of the old Roman farm. Later writers on husbandry all drank from this spring.
ptolemy-almagest-manitius-1912:
Claudius Ptolemy of Alexandria built the ancient world's full system of the heavens in the second century. The Almagest, in Karl Manitius's German rendering of 1912 and 1913, gives that system whole. For some fourteen centuries, this book ruled how men reckoned the sky.

Ptolemy shows, with tables and proofs, how circles set on circles can track the sun, moon, and planets. His star lists and tools let any trained reader cast the heavens for a given date. Manitius's version opened the Greek master to modern German readers. The Almagest stands at the summit of Greek science.
crowley-book-4-part-1-1912:
Crowley set out to write the great textbook of his system, and Book Four opened it in 1912. Book 4, Part I: Mysticism, written with Mary D'Este Sturges, teaches the still half of the work. It is the course in mysticism of his order, the A A.

Posture, breath, and the holding of one thought are taught step by step. Crowley borrows the ladder of yoga, from asana to samadhi, and strips it of cult dress. His aim is plain: train the mind until it can rest on one point. The volume grounds all the magic that follows in the set.
doyle-the-lost-world-1912:
Arthur Conan Doyle sent four men up a lost plateau in South America in 1912, and they found dinosaurs alive. The Lost World is the novel that named a whole kind of tale. Professor Challenger leads the party, loud, proud, and sure he is right.

Apes, pterodactyls, and lost tribes fill the high world above the falls. The book's mix of science, sport, and peril made it a hit at once. Real hunters of unknown beasts took its plot as a kind of map. Fiction and the beast hunt have walked together ever since that year.
dunsany-book-of-wonder-1912:
Small, sharp, and bright with pictures, The Book of Wonder of 1912 is Dunsany's most loved story book. Its short tales are his fantasy at its most packed and pure. Sidney Sime's drawings match the text wonder for wonder throughout.

Thieves, gods, and seekers meet bad ends and strange mercies in a page or two each. The Chu-bu and Sheemish tale, of two fat small gods, is the book's famed jest. No shelf of early fantasy is whole without this volume in its place. It is Dunsany in miniature, at full and lasting strength, a small book with a long life.
hodgson-night-land-1912:
Far in the years ahead, the sun has died in William Hope Hodgson's huge novel The Night Land, from 1912. The last folk of earth live in a vast fort of stone and steel. Great beasts and still, dread forms roam the black waste past its walls.

One man leaves the fort to seek a lost love from a past life. His trek is long, harsh, and full of dread sights. The book helped found the dying-earth tale. Its scale and gloom still stun new fans. Great Watchers stand still for ages past the walls, which adds dread. The love quest at its core keeps the huge tale warm and human.
benson-room-in-the-tower-1912:
E. F. Benson led his set of ghost tales from 1912 with a tale of a room in a tower. A man dreams of the room for years. In each dream a grim host bids him wait for a guest who is long dead. Then he is asked to sleep there in real life.

Benson writes with crisp pace and cold nerve. His ghosts show no soft side. Tales of caterpillars, trams, and blind dread fill the set. It is a high mark for ghost tales of its age, lean and cruel. Benson came from a house of church chiefs and school heads. His cool, patrician voice makes his cruel ghosts feel all the more stark.
petrie-formation-alphabet-1912:
W. M. Flinders Petrie traced our ABC to Egypt in The Formation of the Alphabet, his tract of 1912. Most held that the Phoenicians made the first ABC from scratch. Petrie shows signs in Egypt, some in mines of Sinai, that look like first steps to an ABC long ere their age. Each sign, he claims, grew from a drawn thing.

Charts match sign to sign through the ages. His claim sparked rows, yet parts of it have worn well. The tract is the root text of one school on the ABC's birth. It shows Petrie at his most keen.
odonnell-werwolves-1912:
Elliott O'Donnell ranges the whole wolf lore in Werwolves, his survey of 1912. O'Donnell was a famed ghost hunter of his day in London. His book runs through scores of short parts. Wolf men of old lands sit by fresh tales from guests. One part e'en tells how a man might turn wolf by rite, herb, or curse.

He writes for thrills, with a show man's flair. Sages doubt much of it, yet crowds ate it up. The book is the theme's vast fair ground. It shows the lore at its most lush.
haanel-master-key-system-1912:
Charles F. Haanel sold The Master Key System as a mail course from 1912. The course ran to four and twenty parts, one a week. It taught the New Thought creed that mind makes the world of each man. Haanel wrote for men of trade who sought wealth and calm.

Each part pairs a talk with a drill for the mind. Still thought, clear scenes in the mind's eye, and firm will form the core. Haanel holds that thought draws like to like in the world. The book is a root text of the mind power school of the States.
agricola-de-re-metallica-1912:
Georgius Agricola wrote De Re Metallica in Latin in 1556. Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover gave it English dress in 1912. Hoover was a mine man long past when he took up the task. The book is the great text on mines and metal work of its age.

Twelve books tell of shafts, pumps, ores, and the smelt of each metal. Fine wood cuts show the craft at work, gear by gear. Agricola writes from years at the mines of Bohemia. The Hoover dress, with its rich notes, made the book a prize of the trade.
schopenhauer-world-will-idea-vol-2-1912:
Arthur Schopenhauer wrote The World as Will and Idea as his great work. R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp gave it English dress in three books. Book two holds his attack on the Kant scheme and adds to Books One and Two of the main work. Schopenhauer held Kant the peak of thought past him.

His gripe with Kant turns on how the mind shapes the world it knows. The adds deal with the senses, with thought, and with man's place in nature. Will, blind and blind still, drives all things in his bleak scheme. The book is key to the whole of his dark, clear thought.
schopenhauer-world-will-idea-vol-3-1912:
Book three of Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea ends the Haldane and Kemp set. The book gives adds to Books Two, Three, and Four of the main work. Schopenhauer kept at his one great book all his life. Its fame came late, when he was an old man in Frankfurt.

The adds take up life and death, art and music, and the denial of the will. Saint and monk stand as the mark of the soul that quits the chase. Schopenhauer's prose is clear, fierce, and full of scorn for cant. The book ends one of the great schemes of thought of its age.
cervantes-don-quixote-shelton-1612:
Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote in Spain, and Thomas Shelton made it English in 1612. Shelton's was the first English version, and the first in any tongue but Spanish. Don Quixote, a lean old squire mad on tales of knights, rides out to win fame.

With fat, shrewd Sancho Panza at his side, he fights windmills he takes for giants. Inns become castles and flocks become armies in his wild mind. The pair talk, argue, and grow fond as the joke turns kind. Shelton's brisk prose still reads with speed and fun. Later versions abound, but Shelton keeps the raw early flavor.
dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-19:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote The Brothers Karamazov, his final novel, and Constance Garnett made it English in 1912. Garnett's version became the standard English Karamazov for decades of readers. The book mixes a murder case with vast debates on faith, freedom, and guilt.

Three brothers, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha, clash with their coarse, grasping father. When the old man is murdered, Dmitri stands trial for a crime of passion. Ivan's tale of the Grand Inquisitor asks why men trade freedom for bread and rule. Alyosha, a novice monk, seeks a way to live faith amid the wreckage. The novel's scope and force place it among the world's greatest books.
johnson-ex-colored-man-1912:
James Weldon Johnson published his novel in 1912 without putting his name on it. The narrator is a light-skinned Black man who works as a musician. He grows up in the South, moves north, and later travels to Europe. At each step he faces a hard choice about race and safety.

Over time the narrator decides to live as a white man and give up his music. He marries, works in business, and keeps his past secret. The ending leaves him full of regret for what he traded away. Readers still value the novel as an early and honest look at passing in America.
mann-death-in-venice-1912:
Thomas Mann published Death in Venice in 1912, a German novella about a writer on holiday. Gustav von Aschenbach is a famed author known for discipline and hard work. He travels to Venice and becomes obsessed with Tadzio, a beautiful Polish boy at his hotel. He watches from afar and never speaks to the boy.

A cholera outbreak spreads through Venice while officials hide the truth. Aschenbach stays, decays in spirit, and neglects his health and dignity. Mann sets Apollonian order against Dionysian passion, in Greek terms. The prose is stately and exact. The novella is a perfect, troubling study of art, beauty, and decline.
cornford-religion-philosophy-1912:
F. M. Cornford published From Religion to Philosophy in 1912, a study of how Greek thought began. Cornford argues that early philosophy grew out of religious ritual and myth. Concepts like fate, soul, and nature carry traces of older rites and tribal life. The Milesian thinkers did not break with religion at a stroke.

He traces Moira, or fate, from ritual roots to cosmic law. Mystery cults and Orphic beliefs receive close study. The book is the philosophical charter of the Cambridge ritualist school. Its claims are bold and still debated by classicists. Cornford writes with lucidity rare in such deep waters. It pairs well with Harrison's Prolegomena from the same circle.
cumont-astrology-putnam-1912:
Franz Cumont's Astrology and Religion among the Greeks and Romans appears in J. B. Putnam's translation of 1912. The book prints Cumont's American lectures of 1911. Cumont shows how star worship from Babylon conquered the Roman world. Astrology promised a map of fate written in the heavens.

He traces Chaldean lore through Greek science to Roman emperors and their horoscopes. Religion, science, and superstition blend in his account. Cumont was the leading scholar of ancient mystery faiths. The lectures are brief, elegant, and full of learning. They show why the stars held such power over ancient minds. Modern readers gain a clear door into that world.
loeb-mechanistic-life-1912:
Jacques Loeb was a German-born physiologist who wanted biology run with the strict methods of physics and chemistry. His 1912 book The Mechanistic Conception of Life states that program as a manifesto. Living things, he argues, are machines whose moves can be forced and forecast.

Loeb reports tadpoles and sea creatures made to turn toward light or chemicals by set drives he calls tropisms. He also cites artificial parthenogenesis, eggs made to grow without fertilization by a salt bath. His bold claims thrilled some readers and angered others, but they set a research agenda for decades.
giles-taoist-teachings-lieh-tzu-1912:
Lionel Giles translated Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzu in 1912, giving English readers the third Taoist classic in full. Lieh Tzu is named for a sage who, in legend, rode the wind. Giles's version was the first complete English rendering of the text.

The chapters mix short tales, dialogues, and musings on fate, dreams, and the vanity of striving. A famous passage asks whether a man who dreamed he was a butterfly should trust waking or the dream. The book completes the trio of Taoist works beside the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu.
harrison-themis-1912:
Jane Ellen Harrison was a Cambridge scholar who turned Greek studies toward ritual, art, and the life of the group. Her Themis, published in 1912, studies the social origins of Greek religion. It is the mature statement of the ritualist school she helped to found.

Harrison argues that rite came before myth: the dance and the sacrifice are older than the stories told to explain them. Her title names Themis, the goddess of settled custom, as the force beneath the shining Olympian gods. The book's mix of field reports, vase paintings, and bold theory still provokes classicists.
murray-five-stages-greek-religion-1912:
Gilbert Murray, Oxford's great humanist and translator of Greek drama, published Five Stages of Greek Religion in 1912. The lectures trace Greek faith from early nature worship to late philosophy. Murray writes for general readers in lucid, graceful prose.

He moves from the Olympian gods in their bright order to the failure of nerve he saw in the later ancient world. Mystery cults, astrology, and world-weariness fill his fourth stage before reason makes its last stand. His humane, skeptical survey long served as the standard short account of Greek religion in English. Murray never hides his own loves and doubts behind his learning.
lancre-tableau-de-linconstance-1612:
Pierre de Lancre was a French judge sent by the king to the Labourd country in the Basque lands in 1609. His Tableau de l'Inconstance des Mauvais Anges et Demons, published in 1612, reports the witch-hunt he led there. It is the fullest French demonological report of the Basque trials.

De Lancre describes sabbaths on the shore, dances, feasts with demons, and the testimony of hundreds of accused villagers and children. He believed nearly all of it, and his court sent scores to the stake on such evidence. Historians read his Tableau as both a record of the trials and a window into the judge's own fevered mind.
shahnama-warner-vol-6-1912:
Volume 6 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1912, the sixth of nine volumes of the first complete English Book of Kings. Firdausi's epic, finished around 1010, runs to some fifty thousand couplets in Persian. Arthur and Edmond Warner rendered it for readers who had no other way to reach the whole poem.

The historical shahs take up more of the tale here, with wars against Rome and Turan and the splendor of the Sasanian court. Alexander and other foreign rulers enter Persian memory in Persian dress. The volume shows the epic changing tone as myth gives way to chronicle. It also shows the Warners' steady method: close translation, full notes, no cuts.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-07-1912:
Volume 7 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1912, as Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild, Part 1. James George Frazer turned from dying gods to the spirits of the fields themselves. European harvest customs, gathered from many villages, form the core of the volume.

Frazer described the corn mother, the last sheaf, and mock killings and marriages at harvest time. He argued that farmers once believed a spirit lived in the grain and had to be caught, kept, or killed with care. Examples come from Britain, Germany, Scandinavia, and beyond. Part 1 shows his method working close to home, on customs still alive in living memory.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-08-1912:
Volume 8 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1912, completing Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild. James George Frazer ranged wider here, from European fields to the rice lands and forests of Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The corn spirit of Part 1 gains kin worldwide.

Chapters treat sacred trees, grove worship, and the spirits of wild animals and the hunt. Frazer matched harvest rites across oceans to argue for shared patterns in early religion. Later scholars trimmed his claims, but the gathered customs remain a vast record. The volume closes his long survey of plant and animal spirits in folk practice.
huygens-treatise-on-light-1912:
Christiaan Huygens's Treatise on Light appeared in English in 1912, translated by Silvanus P Thompson from the French work of 1690. Huygens, a Dutch scientist, rivaled Newton in the study of light. Where Newton pictured particles, Huygens pictured waves spreading through an unseen medium.

Huygens explained reflection, refraction, and the strange double refraction of Iceland crystal by waves alone. His principle, that each point of a wave starts fresh waves, still bears his name in physics classrooms. Thompson's version was the first in English, more than two centuries after the original. The book is the founding text of wave optics, clear and brief beside its great influence.
descartes-philosophical-works-haldane-ro:
Volume 2 of Haldane and Ross's Philosophical Works of Descartes appeared in 1912. It holds the Objections and Replies to the Meditations, the great debate that followed Descartes's 1641 book. Learned critics across Europe sent objections, and Descartes answered each in print.

Caterus, Hobbes, Arnauld, and Gassendi pressed Descartes on God, the soul, and the circle in his proofs. Bourdin and others joined the attack. Descartes's replies clarify and sometimes shift his claims under fire. The volume is the essential companion to the Meditations. It shows early modern philosophy being made in argument, on mind, God, and knowledge, by the sharpest minds of the age.
berkman-prison-memoirs-anarchist-1912:
Alexander Berkman published Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist in 1912. Berkman, a Russian-born anarchist in New York, had shot steel magnate Henry Clay Frick in 1892 during the Homestead strike. He served fourteen years in American prisons, most at Western Penitentiary in Pennsylvania.

Berkman told of brutal guards, solitary cells, and the small kindnesses that kept men human inside. He also traced his own change from a would-be martyr to a man who questioned his act. The memoir refuses self-pity and judges the prison system from within. It stands as a classic of prison writing and of anarchist life stories in America.
butler-notebooks-1912:
Samuel Butler, the English writer behind Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, filled private notebooks for most of his adult life. He never meant them for print in this form. After his death, his friend Henry Festing Jones arranged the notes by theme, and they were published in 1912.

The short entries cover art, science, religion, money, and daily life, often in a few dry sentences. Butler mocks Darwin's followers, questions church doctrine, and praises plain common sense. Some notes are jokes; others hold the seeds of his books. Read together, they show one of the sharpest and most contrary minds of his age.
webster-white-devil-1612:
John Webster wrote The White Devil early in his career, and it reached print in 1612. The play draws on recent Italian scandals around Vittoria Accoramboni, a famous beauty murdered in 1585. Its first London production failed, but Webster defended the play in print with pride.

Vittoria is tried for adultery and murder in a corrupt court that already knows its verdict. Her lover, the duke Bracciano, plots fresh murders with the villain Flamineo, her own brother. Poisonings, ghosts, and a storm of revenge follow until nearly everyone of rank lies dead. Webster paints a whole society rotted by lust and ambition. The trial scene, where Vittoria out-faces her judges, is the play's blazing center.
wharton-reef-1912:
Edith Wharton published The Reef in 1912, writing much of it in France, where she then lived. The American widow Anna Leath has settled in a French country house with her stepdaughter. Wharton called it, in effect, a story told almost entirely through shifting feelings and half-spoken truths.

Anna is engaged to George Darrow, a diplomat she loved in her youth. Before the wedding she learns that Darrow recently had an affair with Sophy Viner, the girl now hired as her stepdaughter's companion. Doubt works on Anna like acid as she questions both lovers. Nothing is ever stated plainly, and every talk shifts the ground. Wharton builds her most psychologically intricate novel out of hints, pauses, and dread.
dreiser-financier-1912:
Theodore Dreiser published The Financier in 1912, the first volume of his Trilogy of Desire. He modeled Frank Cowperwood on Charles Yerkes, the traction magnate who built and looted transit empires in Philadelphia and Chicago. Dreiser had covered Philadelphia as a young reporter and knew its machine politics well.

Cowperwood starts as a boy turning a quick profit on soap and rises through banks, street railways, and city loans. He takes a mistress, raids the city treasury with a compliant treasurer, and rides the panic of 1873 into prison. Dreiser treats his predator with fascinated respect, as a force of nature among smaller fish. The Financier is the foundational novel of American capitalism's inner life.
kalidasa-shakuntala-ryder-1912:
Arthur W. Ryder's verse translation of Kalidasa appeared in Everyman's Library in 1912. Alongside Shakuntala it holds Kalidasa's two other dramas, Malavika and Agnimitra and Urvashi, plus three long poems. The Dynasty of Raghu, The Birth of the War-God, The Cloud-Messenger, and The Seasons complete the volume.

Ryder, a Sanskrit scholar at Berkeley, aimed for poems that sing in English as they do in Sanskrit. His Shakuntala became the standard modern counterpart to Jones's pioneering version of 1789. The Cloud-Messenger, a lover's message sent by cloud, shows Kalidasa's lyric gift at its purest. Readers can compare two ages of translation in the library's pair. Ryder's notes stay light, letting the verse carry the learning.
scheible-das-kloster-vol12:
Band twelve, cells forty-five through forty-eight, closed Das Kloster in 1849. Johann Scheible's anthology had run to twelve bands of complete reprints in five years. No other German editor of his century matched that scale in saving folk print from decay.

The last cells hold the usual rich stock: grimoires, Faust books, and Höllenzwänge in full text. Folk charms and chapbooks, the cheapest print of past ages, stand preserved beside them. With this band the cloister door, so to speak, swings shut on a full house. Workers on German magic still enter by Scheible's door, because so many texts live nowhere else.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-4-:
Maudslay's fourth volume of Bernal Díaz's True History, from 1912, covers the siege and fall of Mexico. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, fell in 1521 after a brutal fight across its causeways and canals. Díaz had stood in that fight as a foot soldier, and his old-age account carries the memory in his bones.

One volume of the set, the third, is a portfolio of maps only, so the story runs through volumes one, two, four, and five. In this volume the long campaign reaches its grim peak. Díaz records hunger, loss, and the city's ruin without turning away. It is the conquest's climax told by a man who swung a sword in it.
lamettrie-man-machine-bussey-1912:
Julien Offray de La Mettrie, a French army doctor, published Man a Machine in 1747 and fled two countries for writing it. The Open Court translation of 1912, by Bussey and Calkins, is the text here. Frederick the Great's Eulogy of La Mettrie and extracts from his Natural History of the Soul travel with the main work.

La Mettrie's manifesto denies the soul any life apart from the body's machinery. Thought, feeling, and morals all rise, he argues, from organized matter in motion. Fever, food, and sleep change the mind because the mind is the body at work. The claim enraged church and state in his day. Man a Machine remains materialism's founding firecracker, witty and unrepentant.
eucken-main-currents-1912:
Meyrick Booth's 1912 translation carries the subtitle a study of the spiritual and intellectual movements of the present day. Rudolf Eucken first issued the German work in 1904 as Geistige Stroemungen der Gegenwart. In it the Jena professor and Nobel laureate surveys the forces then shaping modern minds.

Eucken sorts the main currents of his age and weighs what each one offers human life. He asks which movements deepen the life of the spirit and which leave it thin. His judgments favor effort, unity, and inner growth over mere fashion. English readers got here a broad map of European thought around 1900.
boutroux-william-james-1912:
American thinker William James drew readers across the Atlantic, and French philosopher Emile Boutroux was among them. Boutroux published his study William James in French in 1911. Archibald and Barbara Henderson brought the short book into English the next year, in 1912.

Writing as a French spiritualist, Boutroux explains James and his pragmatism to European readers. He presents James's views on truth, belief, and religious life with care and sympathy. At the same time he marks where his own thought parts from the American's. The study shows two traditions in direct talk with each other. It remains a neat period portrait of James.
boutroux-historical-studies-1912:
Fred Rothwell translated a set of Emile Boutroux's French studies on the history of philosophy in 1912. The French title, Etudes d'histoire de la philosophie, states the plan in plain terms. Each study takes up past thought on its own ground. Boutroux was known for close, fair reading of other minds.

In these pages he works through major figures and schools from earlier centuries. He asks what problem each thinker faced and how the answer fit its time. The method treats old systems as live attempts, not museum pieces. Students of Boutroux value the set as a model of his craft. It also records French scholarship of his era.
schiller-formal-logic-1912:
Formal logic claimed to state the pure laws of thought, above human mess and error. F. C. S. Schiller attacked that claim in Formal Logic, published in 1912. The subtitle names logic a scientific and social problem. Schiller, the Oxford humanist, treats logic as a human instrument instead.

He argues that real thinking serves aims, faces risk, and works with rough material. Rules of logic, on his view, are tools judged by how well they guide inquiry. The attack drew sharp replies from defenders of the old logic. His case remains a bold pragmatist challenge. It asks what logic is for.
principia-mathematica-vol-2-1912:
Volume two of Principia Mathematica came out in 1912, from Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell. The first volume had built the logical frame and the theory of classes. This volume turns to cardinal and ordinal arithmetic. Cardinals count how many, while ordinals capture order and sequence.

The theory of series receives long treatment, since order runs through all later math. Step by step, the authors prove results most readers take on trust. Their notation stays dense, and the pace stays slow and exact. The volume holds the middle of a three part work. It shows the logicist program at full stretch. Endurance is the price of entry.
spr-proceedings-vol24-1910-1912:
Parts sixty and sixty one, with an appendix, form volume twenty four for 1910 to 1912. The SPR Proceedings reach thirty years from the founding in this stretch. Telepathy research persists, refined by decades of criticism. The society's case files on apparitions grow by steady additions.

Mediumship reports, led by the Piper record, remain the most argued pages. Physical phenomena receive brief, guarded notices, as usual in this era. The appendix handles society matters and odds of evidence. Volume twenty four shows the archive near its First World War pause. Its contents fed the survival debate for years after. Method and patience mark every report.
schliemann-how-i-found-atlantis-1912:
Readers of the New York American on October 20, 1912, met a bold front-page claim: a young man said he had found lost Atlantis. Paul Schliemann presented himself as a grandson of Heinrich Schliemann, the famed digger of Troy. His letters told of a sealed envelope left by his grandfather, not to be opened lightly.

Inside the tale sit an owl-headed vase, coins of a strange metal, and clues said to point across the ocean. No proof ever backed the story, and it is now read as a famous newspaper hoax. Kept as a record of the Atlantis myth itself, the piece shows how eagerly the lost city gripped the public mind.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol12:
Volume XII of the Journal of Discourses came out at Liverpool in 1869, the year rails finally crossed the continent. Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve, and other elders preach in its pages. Shorthand reporting keeps the sermons close to the moment of delivery, rough edges and all.

A railroad at the doorstep meant new goods, new strangers, and new tests for a separated people. The pulpit answers run through these discourses, mixed with the faith's standing doctrines. Volume XII shows the record doing its work: one voice of counsel for a church entering a changed age.
deussen-system-vedanta-1912:
Paul Deussen spent years building The System of the Vedanta, and Charles Johnston's English translation appeared in 1912 for Western readers. Deussen, a German scholar in Schopenhauer's line, systematized Shankara's Advaita teaching from the Brahma-Sutras with great care. Non-duality, the claim that self and absolute are one reality, organizes the whole account from start to finish.

Western readers gained here their first rigorous map of Vedanta as a working system of thought. Deussen argues from the Sanskrit sources patiently, letting Shankara's logic show its strength on its own terms. The book remains a landmark of German Indology in English dress, dense but rewarding for steady readers.
tosa-diary-porter-1912:
William N. Porter translated Ki no Tsurayuki's Tosa Diary in 1912, a founding work of Japanese literature in English dress. Tsurayuki, a court poet of the tenth century, wrote the diary about 935 in a woman's persona, a bold stroke for his age. It records a sea voyage home from Tosa province to the capital, day by day and poem by poem.

Storms, farewells, pirates feared at night, and grief for a dead child thread the short, luminous entries. The mix of prose and verse set the pattern for Japanese travel writing for many centuries to come. Porter's version carried this tenth-century classic to English readers in faithful, graceful form.
talbot-in-the-shadow-of-the-bush-1912:
Percy Amaury Talbot surveyed the peoples of southern Nigeria in In the Shadow of the Bush, published in 1912. Talbot, a colonial officer in the Cross River region, writes of the Ekoi and their neighbors. Secret societies, juju, in the period's word, and village religion stand at the center of his account.

Masks, shrines, and the law of the Egbo society pass through his observant chapters. Talbot aimed to help rulers understand the ruled, a colonial purpose plain on the page. Even so, his record of Cross River belief and custom remains a rich early source for the region.
lawrence-trespasser-1912:
The Trespasser, Lawrence's second novel, appeared in 1912, drawn from the experience of a friend whose love affair ended in death. Its hero, Siegmund, is a violinist and married man who escapes to the Isle of Wight with his pupil Helena.

For a few days the lovers live in a haze of music, sea, and summer light. Then Siegmund must return to his wife, his children, and the life he fled, and he cannot bear what waits. The novel moves toward its fatal end with the certainty of weather. Already the early Lawrence is present: desire and doom locked together.
conrad-twixt-land-sea-1912:
'Twixt Land and Sea, published in 1912, collects three long sea tales from Conrad's maturity. The title names his lifelong ground: the border where a sailor's ordered ship meets the disorder of shore life.

The most famous is 'The Secret Sharer', in which a young captain hides a fugitive officer in his cabin and finds a double of himself. 'Falk' tells of a captain with a terrible past fighting for love in Bangkok, and 'Because of the Dollars' turns on theft and loyalty in eastern ports. These tales show Conrad's sea world at its richest and most humane.
james-essays-radical-empiricism-1912:
Essays in Radical Empiricism, published in 1912, collects the papers in which James stated his final philosophy. His student Ralph Barton Perry gathered them after James's death, giving form to a system its author left scattered in journals.

Radical empiricism holds that pure experience is the one stuff of the world, and that relations are as real as the things they join. Famous essays here deny that consciousness is an entity at all. The doctrine underlies his pluralism and his late metaphysics. These short papers, dense and bright, are among the most argued-over in American philosophy.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-2-1912:
The second volume of Principia Mathematica, published in 1912, carries Whitehead and Russell's logicist program into arithmetic proper. Here the abstract machinery of volume one is put to work on number itself, step by careful step.

Cardinal arithmetic comes first: what it means for two classes to have the same number of members, defined without counting. Ordinal arithmetic follows, treating order and series with the same rigor. The symbolism remains forbidding, but the achievement is plain. Whole branches of mathematics are rebuilt as logic, step by audited step, in the founding work of modern mathematical logic.
bergson-introduction-metaphysics-1912:
An Introduction to Metaphysics is Bergson's most famous short work, printed here in the 1912 English version by T. E. Hulme. The French philosopher sets out his method in one sustained argument: intuition, not analysis, is how thought reaches reality.

Analysis, Bergson says, circles a thing and gives symbols; intuition enters it and grasps its duration, the flow of inner time. He applies the contrast to the self, to movement, and to life itself. The essay is dense but exhilarating, a key to all his larger books. Hulme's version carried Bergson's fame through the English-speaking world.
bosanquet-individuality-value-1912:
The Principle of Individuality and Value, published in 1912, prints Bosanquet's Gifford Lectures, his full statement in metaphysics. Its subject is the concrete universal: how the whole lives in each part, and how finite selves gain value and meaning within the Absolute.

Bosanquet argues that a self grows by range. The more of the world it can hold in harmony, the more real and valuable it is. Evil and error appear as partial harmonies awaiting completion. The lectures are abstract and elevated in manner. They represent British idealism at its most systematic, delivered in its cathedral style.
perry-present-philosophical-tendencies-1:
Present Philosophical Tendencies, published in 1912, is Perry's critical survey of the warring schools at their height: naturalism, idealism, pragmatism, and realism. Few books map the philosophy of their moment as ably as this one does its own.

Perry expounds each school fairly before judging it from his new realist position. His account of pragmatism, learned from James yet critical of it, is especially valued. The survey's clarity made it a standard reference for students of the period. Reading it now is like reading a dispatch from a battle whose lines still show on the modern map.
hocking-meaning-god-1912:
The Meaning of God in Human Experience, published in 1912, is William Ernest Hocking's philosophy of religion. It is one of the most respected American works in its field. Hocking, a Harvard thinker formed by Royce and James, asks how God can be known in and through experience.

He argues that worship and mystic experience give real knowledge, not mere feeling. God is met as the other self who makes community possible. The book balances argument with testimony drawn from prayer and practice. Its tone is earnest and elevated. It represents American idealism turning, in its last strength, toward religion.
plos-pone-0003412:
Thomas F. Clarke and Patricia L. Clark studied word choice inside genes in this 2008 paper. Most amino acids can be spelled by more than one DNA codon. Some codons are used often, while others are rare. Though rare and common spellings build the same protein, they are not placed at random.

The authors found that rare codons tend to cluster together in genes. These clusters show up across many kinds of organisms. Their placement may affect how a protein folds while it is built. The finding gives gene readers a new pattern to explain.
plos-pone-0003512:
Susanne Diekelmann and co-authors tested what lost sleep does to memory in this 2008 study. People sometimes recall events that never happened, with full confidence. Such false memories grow from strong links to real events. Sleep normally helps sort real memories into long-term storage.

After sleep loss, subjects produced more of these false memories. Their brains seemed to file suggested events as truly seen. Rest appears to guard the line between real and imagined events. The finding warns that tired witnesses and tired students may misremember. False memories matter in courtrooms, where tired witnesses may swear to false events.
plos-pone-0003612:
Yong Wang and Frederick C. C. Leung compared fish and sea squirt genes in this 2008 paper. Sea squirts carry methylation on only part of their DNA. Fish evolved global DNA methylation across the genome. Methylated CpG sites mutate in context-dependent ways over time.

Fish genes showed more GC content at positions flanking CpG sites. Sea squirt counterparts kept lower GC in those spots. The shift may reduce the impact of heavy methylation. Genome chemistry thus records how a silencing system spread. Sea squirts are close kin of backboned animals, which makes the contrast sharp.
plos-pone-0003712:
Po-Shun Lee, Sanjay R. Patel, David C. Christiani, and colleagues published this pilot study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In sepsis, the blood protein gelsolin falls to low levels. Gelsolin normally sweeps up actin, a cell protein spilled into the blood when tissue is damaged. The team studied septic patients.

They tested whether the depth of gelsolin loss tracks with how patients fare. They also checked whether free actin in the blood is a sign of the septic state. The pilot weighs a cleanup protein as a possible marker of sepsis severity and outcome.
plos-pone-0003812:
Shuguang Jiang, Alexis S. Bailey, Devorah C. Goldman, and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The lymphatic system grows out of veins in the embryo and drains fluid from tissues all life long. Little was known about whether circulating progenitor cells help maintain its lining in adults.

The authors investigated whether hematopoietic stem cells, the bone marrow cells that make blood, can form lymphatic endothelium. They report that these stem cells do contribute to the lymphatic lining. The finding extends the blood stem cell's resume well beyond blood itself.
plos-pone-0003912:
Tamami Nakano, Fumitaka Homae, Hama Watanabe, and co-authors recorded brain activity in sleeping babies in 2008. Babies learn links between events and act ahead of what they expect. Behavior studies had shown that skill, but its brain basis was unknown. Imaging work in adults offered hints about how prediction works.

The team measured cortical activity while infants slept and sounds played. Activity rose before expected sounds, showing the brain prepared in advance. That early response suggests prediction machinery works very early in life. The study gives a window on how learning starts in the infant brain.
plos-pone-0004012:
Yufeng Shen, Sumeet Sarin, Ye Liu, and co-authors compared genome sequencing machines in worms in 2008. Whole-genome sequencing promises a shortcut to finding mutations. It could replace slow genetic mapping for mutant hunts. The roundworm C. elegans is a classic model for such work.

Their PLOS ONE article tests two leading high-throughput platforms head to head. Both were used to find chemically induced mutations in worms. Knowing each platform's strengths helps labs pick the right tool. Faster mutant finding speeds gene function studies across biology. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004112:
Peter Vogel, Michael S. Donoviel, Robert Read, and co-authors partially blocked a lipid enzyme in mice in 2009. S1P is a fat signal that modulates many body processes. Its levels must be tightly regulated inside and outside cells. The enzyme S1PL destroys S1P in the final breakdown step.

Their PLOS ONE article reports incomplete S1PL inhibition reshapes immune function. Partial blocking avoided the early death and organ lesions of full loss. That window matters for drugs that target this enzyme. It suggests immune benefits may come without the worst side effects. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004212:
Sumiyo Morita and colleagues published this pancreas study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dicer1 is an essential part of the microRNA pathway, the system of tiny RNAs that fine-tune gene activity. Mice lacking Dicer1 die early in embryonic life, so its role in adult tissues could not be studied with ordinary knockouts.

Using a targeted approach, the team removed Dicer1 in the adult pancreas. They report that Dicer is required for maintaining the adult pancreas. The result shows that microRNAs are not just building instructions for embryos but upkeep instructions for grown organs. The pancreas makes both insulin and digestive juices.
plos-pone-0004312:
Namasivayam Ambalavanan and colleagues published this pilot trial in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inhaled nitric oxide is a proven treatment for pulmonary hypertension in newborns, usually given through a ventilator. The team's earlier animal work showed that nitric oxide given by a simple oxygen hood reduces pulmonary hypertension.

Here they tested the feasibility of that hood delivery in human neonates with an elevated alveolar-arterial difference, a sign of poor oxygen transfer. A hood that works would bring the treatment to babies who are not on ventilators. The pilot checks safety and practicality before any larger trial.
plos-pone-0004412: In 2009, Lind, Odén, and Fahlén tested a diabetes number's true worth. Simulations probed HbA1c's value as a predictor of diabetic complications. The updated mean missed time patterns. The study refines how doctors read the test. The timing of highs mattered.
plos-pone-0004512: In 2009, a Dutch team found good germs guarding rat guts. Probiotics prevented intestinal barrier dysfunction in sick rat pancreatitis. The mixed multispecies germ mix calmed gut oxidative stress. The finding supports probiotic therapy trials soon. The test rats had acute pancreatitis induced.
plos-pone-0004612: In 2009, Adio, Jaud, and Ebbing dissected a tiny molecular walker's stride anew. Kinesin's processivity was fully dissected. The motor proteins stepped along tiny microtubules neatly. The neat study maps the catalytic coupling behind them. The tiny steps were precise indeed.
plos-pone-0004712: In 2009, a team solved a self-chambered protein shredder anew here today. The Pab87 protein-cutter had a built-in chamber. The chambered design was new indeed. The finding maps protein recycling well. The odd build holds a central chamber still.
crabbe-tales-1812:
Twenty-one verse stories make up Crabbe's Tales, published in 1812. The first, The Dumb Orators, mocks men who are bold in safe company and timid when rivals sit near. George Crabbe had spent years as a country clergyman, and his tales draw on lives he had watched at close range.

A miser, a deserted wife, a ruined clerk, and a proud family brought low appear among the figures. Each story lands with a moral point, yet Crabbe keeps clear pity for the people he describes. The book fixed his fame as the poet who told plain truths about common English life.
bancroft-history-us-vol-12:
Ratification fills the second volume of Bancroft's History of the Formation of the Constitution, from 1882. State by state, conventions debate the new frame of rule. Fierce foes warn of tyranny while friends plead for union and strength.

Bancroft follows the close votes and sharp pamphlet wars with care. The republic's birth, in his telling, ends in hard-won consent. His long career closes with the founding completed on paper and in law. The volume serves as a farewell from America's great romantic historian, who spent fifty years telling the one story of liberty taking lasting form.
froude-history-england-vol-12:
Elizabeth's last years fill the twelfth and final volume of Froude's History, from 1865. The Earl of Essex rises, plots, rebels, and goes to the block. The old queen declines in body and spirit, and dies in 1603, ending the Tudor line.

Froude closes his vast epic with the passing of Gloriana herself. Grief, faction, and war with Spain cloud the reign's final seasons. He treats the queen with awe, yet shows the cost of her long rule. The volume ends both a reign and one of the great narrative histories in English, twelve books that made the Tudor century vivid for all later readers.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-12:
Quebec's yearbook for 1637 fills Volume 12, published by Thwaites in 1898. One year of a small colony gets a full, careful annual report. Converts are counted, setbacks are owned, and small brave acts are set down plainly.

Daily life along the St. Lawrence comes through in quiet detail. Readers see sowing, building, teaching, and care for the sick. The priests praise help from France and beg for more hands. No bragging inflates these modest pages from the frontier. Each small gain is weighed with care. Few records show so well how a colony of faith took root in wild country.
dutt-srimadbhagabatam-7-12:
Dutt's Srimadbhagabatam of 1895 gives Books Seven through Twelve in English. The set forms the second half of the Bhagavata Purana, Hinduism's beloved scripture. Books One through Six were not found for this rendering, a gap to note.

Prahlada, the child saint, defies his demon father in Book Seven. Tales of the avatars lead toward Krishna's full, joyful story. Devotion, not mere rite, stands as the path the book commends. Song, story, and deep love of God fill its famous pages. Readers meet the scripture that shaped Hindu devotion for a thousand years past. Its second half carries some of the tradition's most loved stories.
journal-of-discourses-vol-12:
Steel rails reach Utah in the discourses of Volume Twelve, from 1869. The railroad ends the kingdom's long desert isolation at a stroke. Young greets the new era with mingled hope and sharp warning.

The world is coming to Zion now, for good and for ill. Sermons weigh trade, mines, and strangers against the Saints' pure ways. Speakers urge the flock to sell labor, not land or faith. An age closes in these talks, and a riskier one begins. The end of the desert refuge gives the volume its elegiac, wistful pull. Young knows the trains will change his people, and says so.
glanvill-translation-beames-1812:
John Beames translated Glanvill's treatise into English in 1812, opening the oldest book of English law to modern readers. Ranulf de Glanvill, chief justiciar under Henry the Second, wrote the Latin original in the late twelfth century. His work describes the royal courts and writs that were then remaking English justice.

The treatise explains how a claim began with a writ from the king's chancery and moved through the courts step by step. It covers land disputes, inheritance, and the early forms of trial. Beames's version was the first full English dress for a text lawyers had read in Latin for six centuries. The book is often called the common law's birth certificate, and Beames made it legible to the age of reform.
moore-ethics-1912:
Moore published his short Ethics in 1912, restating the doctrine of his Principia Ethica of 1903 for general readers. The Principia had made him the leading voice of a new moral philosophy at Cambridge. The smaller book brings the same teaching to readers without technical training.

Moore holds that good is a simple quality that cannot be defined in other terms, and that we know it by direct insight.
